prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My brother's funeral over, the dark-clothed congregation clots the church doors, a lingering aftermath moving into flat light—the sky low and swollen, a storm siren's long expansive notes, evenly measured, so loud the pauses between ring with aftersound. Used to it, no one here appears alarmed, the church ladies filing into his house bearing heavy covered dishes, the funeral flowers. On the muted television tuned to the weather, a small area of Watch now upgrades to Warning; the words stream across the bottom of the screen calling conditions perfect, this town, this house disappeared beneath the map's isolated lesion, its red edges uneven, stalled. The forecasters rely they say on spotters to confirm what the radar cannot—they call it ground truth; until then no one knows anything for certain beyond this inward watching. The room hums, an airless, crowded hive. Their mouths are full, plates layered—fried chicken, deviled eggs, casseroles, bright congealed salads with fruit suspended inside. All of it dust. I have come here too late, his body gone, already ash. The storm's body could be forming now, tightening from cloud to the gyre that will consume its path, all of it a becoming—spiraling a wall of water, mud, dust, and sand; with dispassion taking up into itself the fence line, a barn—the house beside them spared with the same dispassion. Or this, more likely now: siren silenced, the winds diminishing, the light, afternoon's concession to another dusk—severe, more common truth.

outputs.L2:
After my brother's service concluded, mourners in black gathered thick around the church entrance, their collective grief spilling into the day's flat, colorless light—clouds hanging heavy and bloated overhead, while a tornado siren wailed its steady, measured tones, so piercing that even the silences between blasts seemed to vibrate with lingering echo. Nobody here flinched; this was routine. Women from the congregation streamed toward his house, arms laden with covered casserole dishes and the leftover funeral arrangements.

The television played silently, tuned to weather coverage, showing a small Watch zone shifting to Warning status; ticker text crawled beneath the image proclaiming ideal conditions for severe weather, our town and his house swallowed within an isolated red blemish on the radar map, its jagged borders frozen in place. According to the meteorologists, satellite data alone wasn't sufficient—they needed human observers on the ground, what they termed "ground truth," to verify what instruments merely suggested. Until such confirmation arrived, certainty remained elusive, replaced only by this collective, inward vigilance.

The space buzzed with activity, close and stifling as a beehive. People ate steadily, plates stacked high with fried chicken, deviled eggs, various casseroles, and those sweet gelatin salads studded with suspended fruit. Everything felt reduced to dust somehow. I'd arrived after the fact—his body already reduced to ashes, the funeral itself now history.

Meanwhile, somewhere, a storm system might be organizing itself, clouds condensing into the rotating force that would eventually devour everything in its trajectory—a slow unfolding into a churning column of water, debris, earth, and grit; indifferently absorbing whatever stood in its path—a fence, perhaps a barn—while some neighboring structure escaped destruction through that same blind indifference.

Or perhaps, more likely, the alternative would unfold instead: the siren falling quiet, winds gradually calming, daylight surrendering to another ordinary evening—harsh yet unremarkable, the kind of truth we know all too well.
outputs.L3:
The drive to the church took longer than I'd planned, and by the time I pulled into the gravel lot, it was already over. Not the service—that had concluded on schedule, with the appropriate hymns and the appropriate silences—but my brother himself, reduced now to a gray ceramic urn that sat on a folding table near the altar, catching the thin light from the stained glass windows. I had missed the body. I had missed the chance to see his face one last time, composed and waxen in whatever suit they'd chosen for him, and instead I would have to make do with ash, with the idea of him rather than the fact.

Outside, as I stood there absorbing this, the storm siren began its long, undulating wail, rising and falling like something wounded. I flinched. No one else did. The mourners filing past me toward their cars barely glanced skyward; a few muttered about needing to get the casseroles inside before the wind picked up, but there was no urgency in it, no fear. They had heard this siren a hundred times before, most of which had amounted to nothing more than a few minutes of hard rain and a light show on the horizon. Desensitization, I understood, was simply what happened when the sky cried wolf often enough.

We reconvened at the house—my parents' house, my brother's childhood house—where the kitchen counters groaned under the weight of casseroles and deviled eggs and a ham someone's aunt had glazed with brown sugar, as if grief could be absorbed through sheer caloric volume. In the living room, someone had left the television on, muted, tuned to the local news. I found myself drawn to it the way one is drawn to a wound. A meteorologist stood before a radar map, his mouth moving soundlessly, his hands tracing the edges of a red-rimmed blob that sat directly atop the little dot representing our town. The color had a violence to it that the silence somehow amplified—red the color of warning, of blood, of the taillights receding into the distance.

I stood there long enough that my mother came and put a hand on my shoulder, though whether to comfort me or to redirect my attention I couldn't say. "They always overreact," she said, though her eyes stayed on the screen a beat longer than her words suggested she believed it.

What the map couldn't show, I would learn later from a cousin who fancied himself a weather enthusiast, was the truth of the thing itself—whether the rotation visible in the data was merely a suggestion of danger or an actual, present menace bearing down on actual, present people. Radar could paint the shape of a threat, but it took human eyes, spotters standing in fields and parking lots with their necks craned skyward, phones in hand, to confirm what was real. Ground truth, he called it. Somewhere out there, someone was watching the horizon on our behalf, trying to determine whether we should be afraid.

And so we waited, the way you wait for test results, or for a phone call in the middle of the night—that particular suspended feeling where the outcome exists already, somewhere, unwitnessed, and all you can do is stand very still and let the not-knowing wash over you. I thought about my brother, about the arbitrary cruelty of things—how a storm might touch down on one street and level it to splinters while leaving the house across the road untouched, its windows intact, its flowerbeds undisturbed, as if daring you to make sense of the selection. There was no justice in weather, no more than there had been justice in whatever had stopped my brother's heart at forty-one, quietly, in his sleep, while the rest of us went on about our lives unaware.

Perhaps the storm would find us. Perhaps it would carve its ancient signature into the town, rearranging roofs and trees according to no logic beyond the wind's own restless will. Or perhaps—and this seemed, in the end, more likely, more consistent with how such things usually resolved—it would simply pass, the red on the map fading to green and then to nothing, the siren falling silent, the evening settling back into itself as though it had never been threatened at all. We would eat the ham. We would talk about my brother in the careful past tense that still felt unfamiliar in the mouth. And somewhere above us, indifferent to our grief and our vigilance both, the sky would do what skies do, with or without our watching.
outputs.L4:
The house had filled with the particular quiet that follows a funeral—not silence exactly, but a hum of low voices, the clink of forks against borrowed plates, footsteps moving carefully across the same floors they'd always moved across, as if grief made people suddenly aware of the furniture, the doorframes, the physical facts of a place they thought they knew.

I stood near the kitchen doorway with a paper cup of coffee going cold in my hand and watched them eat. Someone had brought a ham. Someone else had brought potato salad in a dish with a taped-on lid, the kind you don't expect back. My aunt was refilling a bowl of pretzels that didn't need refilling. This is what people do, I thought. They eat because the body insists on continuing even when everything else has stopped.

The television was on in the front room, muted, the way it often is in houses in mourning—on for company, not for content. A storm warning scrolled across the bottom of the screen in that urgent red font, and behind it, the meteorologist gestured at a spinning mass of green and yellow on the radar map, tracking something out over the water that might come ashore or might not. The sound was off, but I could read the shape of his sentences in his hands, in the way he kept glancing at the storm's eye as if it might change its mind before he finished his forecast.

I watched it instead of watching the room. It was easier. The storm didn't know me. It didn't require anything of me—not a hug, not a story about my brother, not the careful arrangement of my face into something that could hold both sorrow and gratitude for casseroles at once. It just moved, indifferent, across a map, deciding nothing yet, capable of becoming a catastrophe or capable of dissolving into ordinary rain somewhere over an inlet no one had heard of.

I thought about how I had missed him. Not missed him in the abstract way people say when they mean they'll think of him fondly—missed him literally, missed the window, arrived at the hospital forty minutes after they had already begun preparing him for the crematorium, so that the last time I saw my brother he was already becoming smoke in some scheduled, administrative sense, already turning into an appointment on someone's calendar. I had pictured, driving there, that I would sit with his body for a while. That there would be time to notice his hands, or the particular stillness of his face, something to carry forward as a final image instead of the school photo we'd propped on the mantel, all gap-toothed and unfinished, a boy who had not yet become the man who died.

Instead there was a form to sign. A kind woman with a clipboard. The word "arrangements" used so many times it stopped sounding like English.

And now here was this storm, tracked and graphed and given a name, promising itself as disaster the way storms do, all spiral and warning color, and I understood, watching it, that it would probably not be a disaster at all. Most of them aren't. They wobble, they weaken, they make landfall as something merely wet and gray, a Tuesday with worse weather than usual. The catastrophe is rare. The diminishment is not.

That was what nobody told you about grief, either—that it was not, in the end, the wailing, cinematic collapse you'd been led to expect by every funeral scene you'd ever watched, every book where loss arrived like a hurricane making landfall exactly on schedule, precisely where the models predicted. It was this instead: a room full of people balancing paper plates, a television flickering with a storm that might or might not come ashore, the ordinary tiredness of a body that had cried too much and was now just standing near a doorway, watching, waiting for something to happen or not happen, while outside the light did what light always does at the end of a day like this—it dimmed, unhurried, indifferent, turning the sky the color of ash, of dusk, of something that had already, quietly, without ceremony, been decided.

# The Warning on the Used Watch

Sarah found the antique pocket watch at an estate sale, tucked away in a velvet-lined box that had seen better days. The seller, an elderly man with knowing eyes, mentioned almost as an afterthought that the watch came with a warning: "Never wind it past midnight."

She laughed at the time, assuming it was simply a quirky sales tactic to add mystique to an otherwise ordinary used timepiece. The watch was beautiful—gold-plated with intricate engravings of stars and moons circling its face. For twenty dollars, it seemed like a steal.

That night, as she prepared for bed, Sarah examined her new acquisition more closely. The warning nagged at her thoughts, but curiosity got the better of caution. It was 11:47 PM. Just this once, she told herself, to see if it still worked properly.

She began winding the watch slowly, watching the second hand tick forward. As the clock struck midnight, something strange happened—the room seemed to shimmer, and for just a moment, she could have sworn she saw her reflection in the watch's glass face smile independently of her own expression.

Sarah quickly set the watch down, her heart racing. Perhaps some warnings, even ones attached to seemingly innocent used items, deserved to be taken seriously. She resolved never to test that particular boundary again, and from that day forward, she only wound the watch during safe daylight hours—a small compromise for keeping such a beautiful, mysterious piece of history in her life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about attending my brother's funeral while a tornado warning siren sounds in the background, blending grief with storm imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Sirens Carried

They buried my brother on a Tuesday when the sky had gone the color of old bruises, green-black and swollen with what was coming. The funeral home director kept checking his phone, kept glancing at the windows like they might tell him something the weather app couldn't.

I wore the black dress that still smelled like the last funeral, and I thought: how quickly a body becomes a season, how grief just keeps returning like weather you can name but never stop.

The siren started during the eulogy. That long, rising wail—the county's warning voice—and for a moment I thought it was for him, thought the sky itself had noticed we were lowering someone made of thunder into the ground. My brother, who slammed doors like weather fronts colliding, who could not enter a room without changing its pressure.

Everyone looked up. Actually looked up, as if the tornado might be visible in that ceiling, in that fluorescent hum, as if the storm and the sorrow were the same thing wearing different coats.

We are taught to seek shelter, to find the low place, the interior room, away from windows. But nobody moved. We sat in our folding chairs with the casket close enough to touch, and the siren wound down into the sound of wind starting to remember what it was made for.

I thought about the trailer trash of my childhood summers, my brother's hand on my shoulder pushing me toward the ditch when the sky turned that same sick color. He knew how to read weather. He knew how to read the air changing. He never learned how to read his own body, the storm building in his chest for years, the funnel cloud of his heart finally touching down on a Sunday morning while I was making coffee three states away.

The rain started as they were reading his favorite psalm—something about valleys, about shadows, about fear no evil though the earth be moved. The rain came down like it had somewhere to be, like it was late for something, and the funeral home's tin roof took up the rhythm, drumming out a percussion no one had arranged but everyone recognized: this is what sorrow sounds like when it finally lets go.

They lowered him as the worst of it passed—the sky lightening from bruise to simple gray, the siren silent now, its work done, its warning honored or ignored, no matter, the storm had come regardless, the storm always comes regardless of our sheltering, our folding chairs, our chosen psalms.

I stood at the grave's edge in mud that hadn't existed an hour before, and I understood: this is how the sky mourns. Not with lightning or dramatic flourish, but with rain that softens ground hard enough to hold a body, that carves out grief-shaped rivulets running toward the drainage ditch he used to push me toward, saying *this way, this way, we have to get low, we have to get to shelter.*

But there is no shelter from this.

There is only the after: sky washed clean and confused about its own violence, sun trying to remember how to shine through clouds still deciding whether they're finished. There is only standing here, in wet grass, in a wet dress, watching them fill in the hole where my brother now lives, permanent as weather, gone as a storm that's passed, leaving nothing behind but the ozone smell of what almost struck, what did strike, what will never stop arriving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary short piece that intercuts a Southern funeral reception—casseroles, church ladies, deviled eggs—with a live severe weather alert on TV.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Sky Was Doing

The television stayed on because no one thought to turn it off, and so between the sympathy cards and the sound of forks scraping Corningware, the man in the blue tie kept saying *rotation*.

Doris Fentress arranged deviled eggs in a spiral on the good platter, the one with the chip on the rim that everyone pretended not to see, and thought: Ellen would have wanted paprika, not just the dusting but a real coat of it, orange as a warning light.

*—a tornado watch now in effect for the following counties—*

The house filled the way houses fill after a death, which is to say entirely, with people standing in doorways because the chairs were full, with pound cakes arriving in twos as though grief traveled in pairs. Someone's casserole dish said HARRIS in Sharpie on masking tape stuck to the bottom, and no one could remember which Harris, there being three families of them at First Baptist alone.

Ruth Ann held the paper plate against her stomach like something that might otherwise fall out of her.

"She looked so natural," said a woman in a cardigan the color of weak tea. This was understood by everyone present to be a lie of the most necessary kind, since Ellen had looked, in fact, like wax, like a rumor of herself.

*—if you are in a mobile home, you need to seek sturdier shelter immediately—*

The green crawl slid along the bottom of the screen behind the muted anchorman, county names scrolling past like a second, smaller funeral procession. Nobody watched it exactly. Nobody could stop seeing it either.

"Bless her heart, she went in her sleep," Doris said, though this too was not quite the truth, the truth being longer and involving a hallway and an ambulance and Ellen's daughter Carol standing in the yard in her housecoat at 3 a.m., but truth at a funeral reception gets sanded down like furniture, all the rough parts smoothed to something you could set a casserole on.

Outside, the sky had gone the color of a healing bruise, greenish at the edges. Someone's grandson pressed his face to the screen door and said, "It smells like a swimming pool," which was as good a description of ozone as any eleven-year-old was going to manage.

*—a large and extremely dangerous tornado was on the ground near—*

"I made the broccoli rice thing," said a woman nobody could place, holding it out like an offering, like something that might be refused. "Ellen always liked it."

Did she? Ruth Ann thought. Ellen had eaten it, certainly, the way Ellen had eaten everything set in front of her at every reception for every death in this town for forty years, funeral food being less about hunger than about hands needing something to do, mouths needing something besides words.

The wind picked up outside in a way you could hear through insulated windows, a low pressure-drop hum that made the good china rattle faintly in the cabinet, an old sound, an old house's complaint.

*—if you can hear this alert and you are not already sheltering, you need to move now—*

Nobody moved. This was the strange thing Ruth Ann would think about later—how the room full of women who had outlived husbands, children, entire decades of this town's slow unspooling, did not so much as glance at the screen. They had already survived worse than weather. They had survived Wednesday night visitation and closed caskets and the particular loneliness of being the last one left who remembered someone's maiden name.

"Ellen's mother made deviled eggs like this," Doris said, though Doris had never known Ellen's mother, who died before any of them were born. But somebody had to keep the recipe alive by attributing it correctly, or falsely, it hardly mattered which.

The lights flickered once, the way lights do before they mean it.

Carol, the daughter, stood in the kitchen doorway with a dish towel twisted in her hands like she meant to wring something out of it, and looked at the muted television, at the map with its angry red blotch crawling toward the county line, toward this exact intersection of road and grief, and thought: let it come. Let it take the tent from the funeral home, the flowers wilting on their wire stands, all of it. Her mother was already gone. What was left to protect?

*—seek shelter now, this is not a drill—*

But it was, in its way, exactly the kind of drill they'd all done before: gathering the food, saying the useless true things, watching the sky for what it might do next while pretending you weren't watching at all. The women moved the good platter to the center of the table, out of the path of the window, just in case, and went on serving deviled eggs into the coming dark, orange with paprika, dozens of them, like something that might, if you weren't careful, start to look like an abundance of small suns going out one by one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an atmospheric flash fiction piece using the meteorological term "ground truth" as a metaphor for uncertainty after a family death.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ground Truth

The forecast said clear skies, but that was three days before Marion stopped answering her phone.

Dana drives the coastal road with the radar app open on the passenger seat, watching the green blob of a system that isn't really there—not yet, not officially. The meteorologists call this "ground truth": what you find when you actually go outside and look, instead of trusting the satellite's guess from two hundred miles up. Model versus reality. The gap between what the instruments predict and what the rain gauge actually catches.

She has been living in that gap for three days now.

The hospice nurse said hours. That was Tuesday morning. The hospice nurse said hours again on Wednesday, apologetic, as if she'd misread her own equipment. Dana has learned that dying, like weather, resists the models built to contain it. You can measure barometric pressure, humidity, the specific gray of a November sky, and still be wrong about when it breaks.

Her brother texts: *any change?* She doesn't know how to answer. The satellite shows one thing. The ground shows another. Somewhere between the algorithm and her mother's shallow breathing is a truth nobody has instruments fine enough to catch.

At the house, she stands in the doorway of the bedroom before going in. This is its own kind of ground truth—the difference between the version of her mother that exists in memory, upright and arguing about parking, and the one breathing in small increments beneath a quilt the color of an overcast morning. The models she's built over thirty-one years don't match what's actually here. They never do, at the end. That's the whole cruelty of it: you prepare for a forecast, and what arrives is weather.

She sits. She takes her mother's hand, which is the temperature of a house with the heat turned down for winter, waiting.

Outside, actual rain starts—no algorithm needed, just the ordinary confirmation of water on glass. Dana watches it collect on the window in fat, undecided drops, each one a small verification of what the sky had only threatened.

Some things you can't know until you're standing in them.

By the time the drops slow to nothing, her mother's hand has gone still in hers, and Dana understands that this is the only kind of truth there is—not the pressure systems or the models, but this: the actual, unbearable now. The ground, and what it finally, quietly confirms.

She sits a long time before she calls anyone. Some readings you have to take alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic, dense paragraph about a rural funeral interrupted by a storm warning, focusing on sensory detail and the tension between ritual and impending disaster.
counterfactuals.output: The pallbearers had just lowered their shoulders beneath the coffin's weight when the sky changed color, that sick green bruise spreading behind the sycamores, and the preacher's voice—which had been rolling out over the mourners like slow black water—caught on the word *dust* and did not finish the verse. Wind arrived first as rumor, a shiver through the black crepe dresses and the borrowed folding chairs, then as fact, snatching the funeral programs from folded hands and scattering them like white birds startled off a wire. Somewhere a phone buzzed against a thigh, then another, then a chorus of them, tinny and insistent beneath the wind's low organ note, each one whispering the same government syllables: *warning, rotation, take shelter now.* The grandmother in the front row gripped her cane and did not move, as if grief itself were an anchor heavier than any wind, while behind her the young ones exchanged glances sharp as lightning, calculating the distance to their trucks. The gravedigger, still waiting with his shovel loose in the red clay, watched the clouds churn like something being born, or unmade, and thought of all the bodies he'd put down easy under blue skies, and how this one might go into ground still singing with static, thunder walking closer on its long legs across the flat fields. The casket sat suspended above the grave on its canvas straps, patient as the dead are patient, indifferent to the living's sudden animal urgency, and for one held breath everyone stood between two ceremonies—the old one of dirt and psalm, the new one of sirens and asphalt—not knowing yet which liturgy the sky had come to perform.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a reflective, image-heavy narrative about returning home too late for a sibling's death, weaving in a tornado watch upgraded to a warning as a symbol of unresolved grief.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Sirens Came Late Too

The radio said *tornado watch* somewhere around Cedar Rapids, and I remember thinking, that's fitting, that's about right—a watch, a waiting, a sky deciding whether or not to become something violent. I drove through Iowa with my hands loose on the wheel and my sister's voice in a voicemail I hadn't listened to yet, saved like a bruise I kept pressing to make sure it still hurt.

By Des Moines it was a warning.

I know the difference now. A watch means conditions are right. A warning means it's already happening, or about to, or has already touched down somewhere you can't see yet. I didn't know that distinction three hours ago. I do now, the way you learn things too late to use them—like the exit for the hospital, like the shape of my brother's name in my mouth when I still believed I'd get to say it to his face.

---

The sky over the interstate had that green underneath, the color of something bruising from the inside. My mother called. I let it ring twice before answering, some animal part of me still negotiating with time, still believing that not-knowing was a kind of mercy I could extend to myself a little longer. She didn't say the word. She didn't have to. The silence after "you should come" had its own gravity, pulling everything in the car—the coffee cup, the gas station receipts, my own ribs—toward a center that didn't exist yet.

I have been the last to know things my whole life. The last to know our father was leaving. The last to know the diagnosis wasn't the good kind. Now I was going to be the last to know my brother, arriving after the knowing was already finished, after the room had emptied of whatever makes a person a person and not just a shape under a sheet.

---

The warning sirens actually went off in Marshalltown. I pulled beneath an overpass with four other cars, all of us strangers doing the same math: how much fear is appropriate, how much is enough. Someone's radio through a cracked window said *rotation observed*, said *seek shelter immediately*, and I sat there with my hazards on thinking: I am so late for this too. The tornado, if it came, would arrive and be gone before I could even understand its shape. Just like everything else this year. Just like him.

I did not cry under that overpass. I want to say I did, because it would make a better story, would make the metaphor land the way I need it to—but I sat there dry-eyed and furious at the sky for taking its time, for making me wait through this small violence when I was already late for the larger one. The wind came sideways. Grit tapped the windshield like something trying to get in. And then it passed, the way these things do, the way grief apparently does not.

---

I got there four hours after.

Four hours: the length of a movie, a flight delay, a long lunch with someone you love. Four hours is nothing and it is everything, it is the exact width of a door closing.

My mother's face when I walked in did not have relief in it. It had the specific exhaustion of someone who has been holding a door open for a guest who arrives after the party has ended, after the other guests have gone home, after someone has already swept the floor. She hugged me like an apology. I didn't know yet who was apologizing to whom.

---

Here is what nobody tells you about a warning: it doesn't mean the storm respects your schedule. It doesn't wait for you to find shelter, to arrive, to say the thing you meant to say for six years and kept not saying because there was always going to be more time, because siblings are supposed to be a renewable resource, an account you can always deposit into later.

I keep thinking about the watch-to-warning upgrade, how there's a moment when the sky shifts from *maybe* to *now*, and how I missed that moment completely, was driving through cornfields with the radio down, was thinking about traffic and not about the actual weather of my brother's body giving up in a room three states away.

---

Months later, I still check the weather obsessively during storm season. Not out of fear, exactly. Out of a need to witness the shift, the watch becoming warning, in real time—as if paying close enough attention now could retroactively make me present for the thing I missed. As if vigilance is a kind of time travel.

It isn't. I know that. The sky does what it does regardless of who's watching, and grief operates on the same terms: indifferent to whether you arrive in time, whether you're standing under the right overpass, whether you've said the necessary things. The storm was always going to touch down somewhere. He was always going to leave before I could shape the words right.

But sometimes, late at night, watching a green blob crawl across a radar map three states away, I let myself pretend otherwise. I let myself believe that if I watch closely enough—if I stay awake long enough, alert long enough—I might finally catch the exact moment when *watch* becomes *warning*, when *before* becomes *too late*, and in catching it, somehow arrive on time after all.

The sirens never sound for what's already happened. That's the cruelest architecture of the whole system.

I am still, in some field in Iowa, four hours away.
